label: Nursing and clinical care
description: The unit and the classroom view of a hospital: charge nurses, nurse managers, rapid response nurses and nurse educators deciding about patients in beds. It builds on the healthcare profile (everything a hospital exercise inherits is repeated here, so a project can run on either) and adds three variants as role sets: a hospital nursing unit, a long-term care facility and a nursing program simulation lab. Plans and references: the CMS emergency preparedness program (42 CFR 482.15 for hospitals, 483.73 for long-term care), the hospital's evacuation and downtime plans, the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model for case studies and the INACSL simulation standards for prebriefing and debriefing. Clinical content is exercise content, never clinical guidance; every patient is synthetic.

vocabulary.facility: the nursing unit (or the long-term care facility, or the simulation lab) and the hospital around it
vocabulary.frontline: staff nurses, charge nurses, nursing assistants, unit clerks, respiratory therapists, rapid response nurses
vocabulary.operationsCenter: the unit's charge nurse desk, backed by the house supervisor and the Hospital Command Center

it: electronic health record (EHR) and the nursing flowsheets
barcode medication administration (BCMA) and the medication administration record (MAR)
bedside monitors and the central telemetry station
laboratory information system and critical value call-backs
nurse call and the patient-room intercom
bed management and patient flow board
the paper downtime forms binder and the downtime computer
learning management system and the simulation recording system (simulation lab)

HVAC and room temperature in the long-term care wing
door access, infant security and duress buttons
fire alarm panels and smoke compartments
high-fidelity manikins and the control room (simulation lab)

roles.name: Chief Nursing Officer (Operations Section Chief)
roles.description: Owns hospital-wide nursing staffing, paper workflows, transfers and bed capacity.

roles.name: Nurse manager / unit director
roles.description: Owns unit staffing, calling in staff, reassigning nurses and the evacuation order of the unit's patients.

roles.name: Charge nurse
roles.description: Owns the shift's assignments, bed moves, triage on a surge and escalation to the house supervisor.

roles.name: House supervisor (nursing supervisor)
roles.description: Owns cross-unit resource moves, diversion input and the first call at night.

roles.name: Staff nurse (RN)
roles.description: Owns assessment, medication administration, escalation, handoff and documentation under downtime.

roles.name: Licensed practical nurse and nursing assistant
roles.description: Owns delegated tasks, vital signs and resident care.

roles.name: Rapid response / resuscitation team nurse
roles.description: Owns the bedside assessment on a call and the transfer to a higher level of care.

roles.name: Infection prevention nurse
roles.description: Owns isolation, cohorting and the notification of public health about an outbreak.

roles.name: Public Information Officer (hospital liaison)
roles.description: Owns family messaging, social media and the press when a unit event becomes public.

roles.name: Nurse informaticist (CNIO)
roles.description: Owns downtime workflows and the return to the electronic record.

roles.name: Long-term care administrator
roles.description: Owns the facility emergency plan, the call to the health department and family communication.

roles.name: Director of Nursing (long-term care)
roles.description: Owns resident checks, staffing, heat and power loss response and evacuation or shelter-in-place decisions.

roles.name: Charge nurse (long-term care wing)
roles.description: Owns resident checks on the wing, medication and fluid rounds, and the resident roster.

roles.name: Maintenance director (long-term care)
roles.description: Owns the generator, cooling, fuel and the call to the utility.

roles.name: Clinical instructor / nurse educator (facilitator)
roles.description: Owns the prebrief, the facilitation, the debrief and the learner assessment.

roles.name: Simulation operator
roles.description: Owns the manikin or standardized patient responses and the pace of the case.

roles.name: Learner team lead
roles.description: Speaks for the learner group in the decisions of a case study.

roles.name: Program director / simulation coordinator
roles.description: Owns the program record: objectives, hours of simulation and the accreditation file.

roles.name: Clinical placement coordinator
roles.description: Owns the students' clinical sites and what happens to a placement when the host unit is in crisis.

outsideParties: CMS and the state department of health
HHS / ASPR and the healthcare coalition
local EMS and the regional trauma system
public health and the local health officer
mediaChannels: a family member's Facebook post about a delayed response
a nurse's anonymous Reddit post about staffing
a student's group chat about the simulation

addedThreatFamilies.label: Unit surge and mass casualty
addedThreatFamilies.description: Casualties or an overflow of patients arrive at a nursing unit faster than its beds, nurses and supplies can absorb; the charge nurse triages, assigns and escalates.

phaseArc.title: Notification
phaseArc.goal: The unit learns that patients are coming, with incomplete numbers.
beats: A call from the house supervisor or ED with a number that will change
A first conflicting estimate of arrivals and their injuries
A bed that is not actually available

phaseArc.title: Unit readiness
phaseArc.goal: Staff, beds and supplies are found or not found before the first arrival.
beats: Discharges to make beds, and a nurse who cannot stay
A supply cart or equipment shortage
A family at the desk asking about their own patient

phaseArc.title: Arrivals and triage
phaseArc.goal: Patients arrive faster than the plan; the charge nurse triages and assigns under uncertainty.
beats: The first arrivals with a mix of START or SALT categories
A patient whose findings do not match the tag
A nurse-to-patient ratio that is now unsafe
A call to escalate the shortage and a decision about who goes first

phaseArc.title: Sustained care
phaseArc.goal: Care continues for hours with shrinking resources and tired staff.
beats: A patient deteriorating while attention is elsewhere
A relief request that cannot be filled
Media or social posts about the surge

phaseArc.title: Decompression and recovery
phaseArc.goal: The unit stands down, restocks and learns.
beats: Transfers and discharges that free beds
A documentation backlog and a missed medication
ENDEX and a hot wash

decisionPointExamples: assign the two experienced nurses to the sickest patients and leave new arrivals with one float nurse, or spread them evenly and accept slower care for the sickest
move a stable patient to a hallway bed to open a room, or hold the room and delay the next arrival
declare that the unit cannot take more patients and tell the house supervisor, or absorb two more and exceed safe ratios
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a vital sign trend that has quietly worsened, a tag whose findings do not match its color, a census board that disagrees with the count at the door
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a missing bed, an empty supply cart, a nurse called away, a monitor that will not pair
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the house supervisor and the emergency department charge nurse
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Write for a charge nurse's desk. Numbers of arrivals and beds change between injects and never add up the first time. Triage categories follow START or SALT findings; never give a patient a category that contradicts the findings unless the inject is meant to show a mistriage. All patients are synthetic.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Unit evacuation (horizontal and vertical)
addedThreatFamilies.description: A unit must move its patients out of a threatened area, horizontally behind fire doors or vertically by stairs and elevators, with equipment, medications and records.

phaseArc.title: Warning and decision
phaseArc.goal: Leadership decides whether and when to evacuate with partial information.
beats: A threat report that is not yet confirmed
A decision to shelter in place or to begin moving the most dependent patients
A call to the receiving hospitals and transport

phaseArc.title: Patient priority and preparation
phaseArc.goal: The unit ranks patients, gathers equipment and prepares the transfer information.
beats: A ranked list that disagrees with the charge nurse's judgment
Ventilator or infusion batteries with limited time left
A patient who cannot be moved safely

phaseArc.title: Movement
phaseArc.goal: Patients are moved and tracked as the situation changes.
beats: An elevator that stops, forcing carries and sleds
Two patients with the same name on the tracking sheet
Staff running out of hands for the most dependent patients

phaseArc.title: Accounting and handoff
phaseArc.goal: Every patient is accounted for and handed off with the right information.
beats: A patient missing from the destination list
Handoffs with medications and allergies missing
Families calling about a loved one's whereabouts

decisionPointExamples: evacuate the neonatal intensive care unit first because it is the most dependent, or hold until transport for incubators arrives and risk the water rising
carry the ventilated patients down the stairs now, or wait for one working elevator and accept a delay
leave one patient who cannot be moved safely with a nurse, or order everyone out
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a battery run-time on a transport ventilator, a tracking sheet that does not match the count, a staircase blocked by smoke
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: an elevator that has stopped, a transport vehicle that has not come, a missing set of medications, a destination hospital that has changed its mind
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the hospital command center, local EMS and the receiving hospitals
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Horizontal movement is normally considered before vertical movement. Dependent patients (ventilated, infants, bariatric) take more staff and time. The evacuation order is a ranked list with reasons, not a formula. Keep patient tracking exact: names, bed numbers and destinations must stay consistent between injects.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Outbreak on a unit
addedThreatFamilies.description: An infection spreads through a unit (C. difficile, norovirus, a respiratory virus); the unit isolates, cohorts, staffs and notifies.

phaseArc.title: Cluster
phaseArc.goal: A few similar cases appear; nobody is sure it is an outbreak.
beats: Two patients with the same symptoms reported at shift change
A lab result that is positive but not yet reported
A visitor who was sick

phaseArc.title: Recognition and isolation
phaseArc.goal: Infection prevention declares an outbreak and the unit isolates patients.
beats: A precaution sign nobody remembers whether it was posted
Not enough single rooms, and a decision to cohort
A shortage of gowns or the right cleaning product

phaseArc.title: Staffing and spread
phaseArc.goal: Staff fall ill or must be reassigned, and the outbreak reaches a second unit.
beats: Staff calling out sick
A float nurse moving between cohorts
Visitor restrictions and unhappy families

phaseArc.title: Notification and recovery
phaseArc.goal: Public health is notified and the unit returns to normal.
beats: A call from the health department
A terminal cleaning and clearance decision
A press inquiry and a hot wash

decisionPointExamples: close the unit to admissions, or keep admitting and cohort within it
assign dedicated staff to the isolation cohort and leave the rest short, or float staff between cohorts and risk spread
notify public health now with incomplete data, or wait for the confirming lab result
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a lab result listing the organism, a pattern of room numbers, a shared piece of equipment or meal
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: isolation supplies running out, a lab backlog, a unit with no single rooms
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: infection prevention and the local health department
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Precautions are specific to the organism (for example contact precautions with soap and water for C. difficile, since alcohol hand rub does not kill spores). Do not invent attack rates or outbreak definitions; use the plan and documents the project supplies.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Medication error and disclosure
addedThreatFamilies.description: A medication error reaches a patient; the unit responds clinically, reports it and discloses it to the patient and family.

phaseArc.title: Discovery
phaseArc.goal: Someone notices that something is wrong with a medication.
beats: A second nurse notices a discrepancy at a double check
A patient who looks different after a dose
A pharmacy call about a dispensing record

phaseArc.title: Clinical response
phaseArc.goal: The patient is assessed and cared for first.
beats: A rapid response call or a call to the provider
An antidote or monitoring plan
Pressure from the unit to keep moving

phaseArc.title: Report and disclosure
phaseArc.goal: The event is reported and the disclosure conversation is planned and held.
beats: The event report and who files it
A disclosure lead assigned and the first conversation within the target time
A family member's hard questions

phaseArc.title: Learning
phaseArc.goal: The system, not only the individual, is examined.
beats: A look at the process, device and staffing causes
Support for the nurse involved
A decision about reporting outside the hospital

decisionPointExamples: disclose to the family now with what is known and say more will follow, or wait for the review to finish
send the nurse home after the event, or keep them on with a buddy and risk another error
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a barcode scan log, a pharmacy dispensing record, a look-alike label
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a downtime period with no barcode scanning, a shortage that forced a substitution, an interrupted double check
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the provider, pharmacy and the risk manager
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Keep a just-culture tone: the system and the process are examined, not only the individual. Doses and routes must be plausible for the named drug; do not present the exercise as a drug reference. The disclosure conversation has a lead, a target time and a plan for what is said.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Staffing crisis and agency nurses
addedThreatFamilies.description: Call-outs, a sudden census rise or a strike leave a unit short of nurses; the manager fills gaps with agency and float staff and manages safety and morale.

phaseArc.title: The gap appears
phaseArc.goal: The shift starts short and the number is worse than expected.
beats: Call-outs before the shift
A census higher than predicted
A first ratio exceedance

phaseArc.title: Filling the gap
phaseArc.goal: The manager and house supervisor try to staff the shift.
beats: Agency nurses who are unfamiliar with the unit
A float nurse who is not competent for the unit
A request for mandatory overtime

phaseArc.title: Safety under strain
phaseArc.goal: The unit prioritizes care and watches for harm.
beats: A patient who waits too long
A missed medication or assessment
A nurse who says the assignment is unsafe

phaseArc.title: Escalation and recovery
phaseArc.goal: The shortage is escalated and the unit stabilizes.
beats: A call to the CNO and a closure decision
A union or board of nursing question
A debrief on what to change

decisionPointExamples: close beds and hold admissions to keep ratios safe, or accept patients and stretch the team
use an agency nurse without unit orientation on a high-acuity assignment, or leave the assignment short
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a staffing grid showing needed versus scheduled, an acuity score trend, a ratio count on the board
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: an agency that cannot supply a nurse, a badge that does not work for a new nurse, an overtime limit
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the house supervisor and the staffing office
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: State required ratios only as the plan or documents give them; ratio law varies by state. Use a staffing grid with needed, scheduled, called-in and agency counts that add up.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Active threat or violence on a unit
addedThreatFamilies.description: A violent person or an armed threat reaches a nursing unit; staff protect patients, lock down and call for help.

phaseArc.title: Warning signs
phaseArc.goal: Behavior escalates and the unit notices.
beats: A visitor or patient with escalating threats
A call to security that arrives late
A nurse who hesitates to call

phaseArc.title: The event
phaseArc.goal: The threat becomes violence or a weapon, and staff act.
beats: A duress button, a code announcement
Patients who cannot move
Doors that need to be locked and some that cannot

phaseArc.title: Protect and respond
phaseArc.goal: Staff protect patients while law enforcement arrives.
beats: A nurse hurt and a patient in need
Law enforcement who need a unit map
Families calling and social media posts

phaseArc.title: Aftermath
phaseArc.goal: Care resumes and staff are supported.
beats: Accountability for patients and staff
Support for staff
A media statement and an event report

decisionPointExamples: lock the unit and keep patients in rooms, or begin moving the patients nearest the threat
confront the person to protect a patient, or retreat and call for help
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a prior behavior alert in the chart, a duress call log, a visitor badge record
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a door that does not lock, a duress button that did not reach security, patients who cannot be moved
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: hospital security and local law enforcement

decisionMustMention.description: the decision should involve security or law enforcement

addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Do not describe weapon details or tactics beyond what is needed for decisions. Patients who cannot move are a central problem. Include a content notice for the facilitator.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Downtime care with paper charts
addedThreatFamilies.description: The electronic record, the medication system or the monitors are unavailable, and the unit gives care on paper.

phaseArc.title: Outage
phaseArc.goal: Systems go down and the unit decides it is a downtime.
beats: A screen freezes in the middle of a medication pass
A conflicting message about how long it will last
The downtime binder is in a locked cabinet

phaseArc.title: Paper workflows
phaseArc.goal: The unit switches to paper for orders, medications and results.
beats: A paper MAR that is missing a recent order
A lab result that must be called
A handoff on paper that loses a detail

phaseArc.title: Sustained downtime
phaseArc.goal: Fatigue and workarounds appear.
beats: A late medication and a duplicated dose risk
An unlabeled specimen
Staffing stretched by runners

phaseArc.title: Recovery and back-entry
phaseArc.goal: Systems return and paper is entered without losing information.
beats: Back-entry backlog
Discrepancies between paper and the record
A debrief on what worked

decisionPointExamples: hold non-urgent medications until the system returns, or give from the paper MAR with extra checks
divert new arrivals, or admit and accept the risk of incomplete records
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a discrepancy between paper and verbal orders, a result that arrived only by phone, a medication due time that passed
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: printers that are out of paper, the downtime computer that is not updated, a runner shortage
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the nurse informaticist and the hospital IT command
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Use the downtime forms of the clinical systems toolkit where it is on (downtime MAR, order forms). Show what is lost on paper: timing, allergies, previous doses.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Heat and power loss in long-term care
addedThreatFamilies.description: A power failure takes cooling or heat from a long-term care facility; staff check frail residents, manage fluids and decide whether to shelter in place or move residents.

phaseArc.title: Outage begins
phaseArc.goal: Power or cooling is lost and the first estimate is optimistic.
beats: A utility estimate that keeps changing
A generator that powers only some of the building
A temperature that is rising

phaseArc.title: Resident checks
phaseArc.goal: Staff check frail residents and the room temperatures.
beats: A resident with a fever and dry mouth
Residents on oxygen concentrators and powered beds
A fan and fluid plan that exhausts the staff

phaseArc.title: Shelter or move
phaseArc.goal: The director decides whether to move residents.
beats: A neighboring facility that is also affected
A transport shortage
Families arriving to take residents home

phaseArc.title: Outcomes and notification
phaseArc.goal: Residents are accounted for and authorities are notified.
beats: Hospital transfers and a resident who dies
A call to the health department that came late
Press at the door

decisionPointExamples: transfer the most frail residents to the hospital now, or keep them and check them every 30 minutes
call the health department and the state now with an incomplete picture, or wait until the facility knows more
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: an indoor temperature log, a resident check sheet, a fuel gauge on the generator
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a generator that runs out of fuel, an elevator that is down, a shortage of staff who cannot reach the facility
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the county emergency manager, the health department and the utility
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Residents are frail and many cannot tell staff they are in trouble. Check frequency, fluids and room temperature are the key facts. Residents and the facility are fictional. Include a content notice for the facilitator when deaths are part of the scenario.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Clinical event (case study)
addedThreatFamilies.description: A single patient's story unfolds: a deteriorating patient, a fall or workplace violence. Each stage is a decision point aligned to the Clinical Judgment Measurement Model.

phaseArc.title: Presentation
phaseArc.goal: The patient and their baseline: who they are, what brought them here, what is normal for them.
beats: History, medications and allergies
A first set of vital signs and labs
A concern from the patient or family

phaseArc.title: First assessment
phaseArc.goal: Subtle cues that matter appear among many that do not.
beats: A trend rather than a single abnormal value
A distracting finding
A request to the learner to select relevant cues

phaseArc.title: Change in condition
phaseArc.goal: The patient changes and the learner must analyze and prioritize.
beats: New vital signs that cross a trigger
A new lab or finding
Competing explanations to rank

phaseArc.title: Escalation
phaseArc.goal: The learner acts and communicates.
beats: A call to the provider or a rapid response with a structured message (SBAR)
A delayed or partial response
A family question

phaseArc.title: Treatment and reassessment
phaseArc.goal: The learner evaluates whether the action worked.
beats: New values after an intervention
A decision to continue, change or escalate
A second problem

phaseArc.title: Handoff and debrief
phaseArc.goal: The learner hands off the patient and reflects.
beats: A handoff to the receiving unit or team
A read-back with an omission
A debrief with a check-in

decisionPointExamples: call the provider now with a concerning trend, or recheck vital signs in 15 minutes
start the treatment within the nurse's scope while waiting for the team, or wait for the order and lose time
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a vital sign trend, a lab value against its reference range, a change in mental status, an early warning score that crossed a trigger
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a provider who does not call back, a monitor with a loose lead, a missing order
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the provider and the rapid response team
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Write one coherent synthetic patient: age, history, medications and allergies stay the same in every stage, and vital signs and labs follow one trajectory. Name the clinical judgment step each prompt tests (recognize cues, analyze cues, prioritize hypotheses, generate solutions, take action, evaluate outcomes). Do not copy examination items. Exercise content, not clinical guidance.

noiseExamples: a visitor asking where the cafeteria is
a call bell from a room with a patient who wants the television changed
a supply cart restock that arrives on the wrong floor
a badge reader at the staff entrance that stops working
a pharmacy delivery that is for another unit
pressureExamples: a family member's Facebook post saying nobody has been to the room in an hour
a physician asking why the patient's medication is late
the house supervisor asking for two nurses for another unit
a nurse telling the manager the assignment is unsafe
a reporter asking whether the unit is short of nurses
the health department asking for a line list within the hour
